impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents, which cover methods of treating headache with humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. The jury had found willful infringement by Lilly and no invalidity, and the appellate court reinstated those findings. This decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent protection covering biologic drug classes defined by functional characteristics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain and enforce broad claims covering classes of biologic therapeutics (such as antibody-based drugs), supporting robust IP protection for biologics innovators.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar developers face increased risk that functionally-defined biologic patent claims will survive validity challenges, potentially delaying market entry and competition.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages models and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award in a dispute over misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. It also reversed the district court's reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating the original jury verdict. The court affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens trade secret holders' ability to present broader damages theories at trial and protects jury verdicts on contract damages from aggressive judicial reduction.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face heightened exposure to trade secret misappropriation liability and potentially larger damages awards.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit alleging that EOFlow misappropriated trade secrets related to its insulin patch pump through hired former employees.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict and damages judgment in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA's statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. Despite evidence that former Insulet employees shared proprietary CAD files, design information, and algorithms with EOFlow, the court found Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation too early for its 2023 filing to be timely.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's limitations period, providing a powerful defense when plaintiffs delay filing.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face significant risk of losing claims if they do not act promptly upon learning of potential misappropriation, even when the full scope of the theft is not yet known.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that each of four asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether inventorship on related patents should be corrected.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret claims, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known. The court vacated the reasonable royalty award, exemplary damages, and permanent injunction. It also reversed on patent invalidity, finding that the alleged inventor's contribution of generally known ideas could not constitute an inventive contribution.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether asserted trade secrets are truly protectable, requiring plaintiffs to clearly demonstrate the information was not generally known.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs face greater difficulty sustaining claims when the allegedly secret information overlaps with generally known concepts in the field, even after obtaining favorable jury verdicts.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and in striking certain damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement of the '836 patent relating to multicore processor task allocation, finding genuine issues of material fact regarding extraterritorial application and doctrine of equivalents. The court also addressed the propriety of striking damages theories for inadequate disclosure in patent contentions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of method claims involving multinational technology operations may have greater ability to survive summary judgment on extraterritoriality grounds.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies operating globally face continued uncertainty about when domestic patent infringement liability attaches to processes with components or steps occurring abroad.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly estopped Valve under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) from asserting two invalidity grounds in litigation that were not raised in a prior inter partes review petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel by requiring more rigorous analysis of what a skilled searcher reasonably could have discovered.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers retain broader ability to assert invalidity defenses in district court litigation even after IPR proceedings, as courts must carefully evaluate whether prior art was reasonably discoverable without hindsight.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face weakened estoppel protections following IPR, meaning defendants may raise additional invalidity challenges in litigation that were not included in their IPR petitions.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' between a provisional and non-provisional patent application constituted correction of an obvious typographical error entitled to the provisional's priority date, or added new matter breaking the priority chain.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's '953 patent as anticipated by Pfizer's public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid). The court held that the change from C2 to C1 in the substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error, breaking the priority chain to the earlier provisional application and allowing Pfizer's intervening disclosure to serve as anticipating prior art.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical companies benefit from strict priority-date rules that prevent competitors from retroactively broadening patent claims through alleged typographical corrections to capture commercially successful compounds.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent applicants face severe consequences from even minor drafting errors in provisional applications, as changes to chemical formulas or ranges may be treated as new matter that breaks priority chains.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a jury verdict form containing a single infringement question covering all asserted patents, combined with flawed jury instructions on patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, required vacatur and a new trial.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgment, finding that a single-question verdict form covering all asserted patents made it impossible to determine which patents the jury found infringed. The court also remanded for further proceedings on § 101 eligibility of certain patent claims. The decision affirms that some building automation system wireless communication patents survive abstract idea challenges under Alice step one.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies defending against multi-patent assertions benefit from the requirement that verdict forms separately address infringement for each patent, preventing ambiguous general verdicts.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders risk having favorable jury verdicts vacated and costly retrials ordered when verdict forms fail to separately identify which patents are infringed.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices are patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case qualified as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection and sharing patent claims were directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional. The court found the claims directed to the abstract idea of collecting, processing, and sharing farming data, with the recited hardware components being generic.
impacts.positiveImplications: Ag-tech and IoT companies accused of infringing data collection patents benefit from continued strict application of Alice/Mayo to claims reciting generic hardware performing data gathering and processing functions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents on data collection and processing systems in agriculture and other industries face heightened risk of invalidation under § 101, and may also face fee-shifting if cases are deemed exceptional.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent owners who retain the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights have constitutional standing to bring infringement claims despite having granted an exclusive license to a third party.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain meaningful exclusionary rights—including the right to sue third parties for infringement and to control sublicensing—have Article III standing to bring patent infringement suits even after granting an exclusive license. The decision clarifies the standing requirements for patentees who split rights with licensees.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license rights while retaining enforcement authority benefit from clear confirmation that such retained rights provide constitutional standing to sue infringers independently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential jurisdictional defense, as patent owners with retained exclusionary rights will more readily survive standing challenges even when an exclusive licensee exists.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment regardless of personal knowledge, and whether the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that prior art sales expressly disclose a device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representatives may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment and that the on-sale bar does not require express disclosure of a prior art device's functionality—only that the device was sold and embodied the claimed invention. The court also held that computer source code is not hearsay when offered as machine instructions rather than human assertions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent challengers benefit from broader admissibility of corporate representative testimony about historical product sales and from confirmation that prior commercial sales of embodying devices trigger the on-sale bar without requiring functionality disclosure.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased invalidation risk, as prior sales of products embodying claimed inventions can be proven through corporate representative testimony even when original employees are unavailable.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims relating to non-uniform signal constellations in communication systems while affirming eligibility for others. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages, including the admissibility of the patentee's damages expert testimony. The split outcome provides guidance on when digital communication optimization patents survive § 101 challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the digital communications space benefit from confirmation that some optimization-based patent claims survive § 101 challenges and that damages expert testimony may be admitted on reasonable methodologies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing communication standards face continued litigation risk from patents on signal processing optimizations, with eligibility determinations remaining unpredictable.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner can correct inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) when it cannot locate an omitted coinventor, and whether failure to name all coinventors renders patents invalid.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents naming only two of four coinventors were invalid due to incorrect inventorship, and upheld the denial of the patent owner's motion to judicially correct inventorship under § 256(b). The court found that the patent owner's inability to locate the missing coinventor did not excuse the inventorship error. This decision highlights the critical importance of properly identifying all coinventors, especially when working with overseas collaborators.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can challenge patent validity based on omitted coinventors, providing a powerful defense when the patent holder failed to properly identify all contributors to the invention.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign manufacturers on product development face serious patent invalidation risk if overseas contributors to the invention are not properly identified and named as coinventors.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination should be vacated when a non-party to the underlying litigation filed IPR petitions on the same day as the real party in interest's statutory deadline, and whether the Board's obviousness analysis was legally sufficient.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that all challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent were unpatentable as obvious and remanded for further proceedings. The court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR based on the time-bar question. The decision raises significant questions about third-party IPR petitions filed at the statutory deadline of parties involved in related litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer appellate scrutiny of PTAB obviousness determinations, potentially limiting the effectiveness of IPR challenges to commercially significant patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR proceedings to challenge competitor patents face risk that PTAB invalidity findings will be vacated on appeal for insufficient analysis.

impacts.caseName: Fuente Marketing Ltd. v. Vaporous Technologies, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the TTAB erred in finding no likelihood of confusion between a standard character 'X' trademark for cigars and a stylized X-with-dot mark for oral vaporizers, despite overlapping trade channels.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the TTAB's dismissal of a trademark opposition, finding no likelihood of confusion between Fuente's registered standard character 'X' marks for cigars and Vaporous's stylized X-with-dot mark for oral vaporizers. Despite finding that the goods, trade channels, and classes of purchasers overlapped, the Board's determination that mark dissimilarity outweighed these factors was upheld.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses applying for stylized marks can coexist with existing simple character marks in related product categories where the marks are sufficiently dissimilar in overall commercial impression.
impacts.negativeImplications: Owners of simple character marks (like single letters) face difficulty blocking stylized variations even in closely related product markets.
